Both alloys exhibited very low corrosion rates (< 35 micron per year) and retained mechanical strength with strength reduction factor (𝛾) defined as the ratio of yield strength of molten sulfur exposed welded coupons to that of unexposed unwelded coupons greater than 0.95. The chemical analysis confirmed the effectiveness of the cleaning method, with residual sulfur levels reduced to < 1 wt.% for all but one coupon. Optical microscopy results showed that in both polished and etched states, the damage was limited to the surface of the samples. Grain sensitization was visible in the heat affected zone, but nothing more significant than what would be expected to have formed from the welding process. Taken together, corrosion testing of welded and stressed components indicates that the system can achieve lifetimes of ≥20 years under expected operating conditions. VELOCITI Lab Voucher Program (400oC molten sulfur) Element 16 was selected for the DOE Vouchers to Enable Laboratory and Organizational Collaboration for Innovation and Technology Improvements (VELOCITI) program as an add-on to this SETO project. As discussed in the previous section, corrosion and mechanical durability testing up to 300oC in molten sulfur showed that stainless steel 316L and 304L exhibited corrosion rates below 35 microns per year. In the VELOCITI lab voucher, Element 16 collaborated with National Renewable Energy Lab (NREL) to explore and identify suitable candidate materials for high temperature molten sulfur TES operating up to 400 °C. Increasing the charge temperature to 400 °C enables operation at the typical output temperature of commercial parabolic trough CST technology with thermal oil heat transfer fluid and decrease the sulfur TES cost for IPH applications between 120-200 °C due to increase in energy density since molten sulfur can be thermally cycled over a wider temperature range. Corrosion and mechanical testing of A516-Gr70 carbon steel with the amorphous Si coating, SS 304L, SS 316L, and SS 347L showed that SS 304L and SS 347L exhibited the best corrosion resistance, with corrosion rates of approximately 100 microns per year in molten sulfur at 400°C after 1000 hours of exposure. Considering material cost difference between SS 304L and SS 347L, SS 304L was identified as the more cost- effective option. From the mechanical strength perspective, 1000 hours of exposure to molten sulfur at 400°C did not substantially affect the ultimate strength of any of the four materials, likely due to the corrosion effect being limited only to the first tens of microns at the material’s surface. Detailed results and analyses are presented in Ref. [28].
